questions.question: Q: What topics does Paper 2 of OCR J271 cover?
questions.correctAnswer: Paper 2 Section A covers the Law of Tort: negligence (duty of care, breach, damage, occupiers' liability), nuisance and remedies. Section B covers two optional topics chosen by the school — these may include the Law of Contract, Consumer Protection, Employment Law, Rights and Responsibilities, or Criminal Law in Context. Check with your teacher which options you are studying.

questions.question: Q: How should you approach a negligence scenario in Paper 2?
questions.correctAnswer: Use ILAC: identify the legal issue as potential negligence. State the law: duty of care (apply the Caparo test — foreseeability, proximity, fair just and reasonable), breach (the standard of the reasonable person, relevant cases), and damage (factual causation using the 'but for' test, legal causation and remoteness). questions.question: Q: What is the key difference between Paper 1 and Paper 2 technique?
questions.correctAnswer: Paper 1 focuses on the legal system and criminal law, requiring knowledge of structures, processes and criminal elements. Paper 2 focuses on civil law (tort and optional topics), requiring more emphasis on civil liability, the balance of probabilities standard and remedies. questions.question: Q: Why are case authorities particularly important in Paper 2?
questions.correctAnswer: The law of tort is heavily case-based — the principles of duty of care, breach and damage have been developed through judicial decisions. Key cases like Donoghue v Stevenson, Caparo v Dickman and Bolitho define the legal tests. Citing these cases demonstrates understanding of how the law works and supports your application of legal rules to the scenario facts.

questions.question: Q: How should you handle the optional topics in Section B?
questions.correctAnswer: Only revise the two optional topics your school has chosen — confirm this with your teacher well before the exam. For each option, learn the key legal principles, important cases and statutes, and practise applying them to scenarios. Use the same ILAC and evaluation techniques as for Section A. Do not attempt questions on options you have not studied.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response How should you approach a negligence scenario in Paper 2 of OCR J271 GCSE Law? (15 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: When approaching a negligence scenario in Paper 2, use the ILAC method systematically. First, identify the Issue: the question is whether the defendant is liable in negligence for the claimant's injuries or loss. Second, state the Law: negligence requires three elements. For duty of care, apply the Caparo v Dickman three-stage test — was the claimant a foreseeable victim (Donoghue v Stevenson), was there a proximate relationship, and is it fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty? For breach, state that the defendant must meet the standard of the reasonable person — what would a reasonable person have done in those circumstances? If the defendant is a professional, the Bolam test applies: the standard is that of a reasonably competent practitioner in that field, though Bolitho adds that the court must be satisfied the professional opinion is logical. For damage, establish factual causation using the 'but for' test — would the damage have occurred but for the defendant's breach? Then check legal causation: is the damage too remote? Under the Wagon Mound test, only damage that is a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the breach is recoverable. Third, apply the law to the facts: use every relevant detail from the scenario. For example, if the scenario says the defendant was a doctor who failed to read a patient's notes, apply the Bolam test to the specific facts — a reasonable doctor would have read the notes, so there is a breach.
